info.name: UNTP RI — Zitadel Integration
info.description:
# UNTP RI — Zitadel Integration

This collection helps you connect to the UNTP Reference Implementation (RI) using Zitadel for authentication.

## How it works (the big picture)

Think of the RI like a building with locked rooms (tenants). To get in, you need:
1. **A key** (service account credentials) — your client_id and client_secret
2. **A badge** (access token) — you swap your key for a temporary badge at the Zitadel front desk
3. **A room assignment** (tenant) — your badge says which room you belong to

Without all three, you can't get in. This collection automates the whole process.

## Getting started

1. **Import** this collection into Postman (File → Import)
2. **Click the collection name** → go to the **Variables** tab
3. **Fill in your values** (see table below)
4. **If you're an integrator** (you received credentials from an admin): skip to the "Integrator" folder and run "Get Access Token" first
5. **If you're an admin** (you manage Zitadel): use the "Admin" folder to create tenants and service accounts

## Variables you need to set

| Variable | What is it? | Who sets it? | Example |
|----------|-------------|-------------|--------|
| `zitadel_url` | The URL of your Zitadel instance | Admin gives you this | `https://auth.labs.pyx.io` |
| `project_id` | The Zitadel project ID (acts as the "audience" for tokens) | Admin gives you this | `362233591867899919` |
| `client_id` | Your service account username | Admin gives you this | `ri-service-account` |
| `client_secret` | Your service account password | Admin gives you this (one-time!) | `G3n3r4t3d...` |
| `ri_url` | The URL of the Reference Implementation | Admin gives you this | `https://ri.labs.pyx.io` |
| `zitadel_pat` | Admin-only: personal access token for managing Zitadel | Only admins need this | `eyJ...` |
| `access_token` | You don't set this — it's auto-filled when you run "Get Access Token" | Auto | — |
| `sa_user_id` | You don't set this — it's auto-filled when an admin creates a service account | Auto | — |

item.name: Admin — Tenant & SA Provisioning
item.description:
# Admin — Setting up tenants and service accounts

This folder is for **Zitadel administrators only** (the people who manage the identity provider).

You need to set these variables first:
- `zitadel_pat` — your admin access token for Zitadel
- `project_id` — the Zitadel project ID

## When do I use this?

Every time a new organisation needs API access to the RI, you run these 4 requests **in order**:

1. **Create Tenant** — makes a new "room" (tenant) in the system. The `tenant` value you set ends up in the `groups` claim of the JWT.
2. **Create Service Account** — makes a new "user" (machine account) that can log in
3. **Generate Client Credentials** — creates the username/password for that account
4. **Assign Tenant to SA** — assigns the account to the room. This is what puts the tenant into the token's `groups` claim.

Then you hand the `client_id`, `client_secret`, `project_id`, and URLs to the integrator. They use the "Integrator" folder from there.

request.description:
# Create a Tenant

This creates a new tenant in the system. The `tenant` value you set (e.g., `org-acme`) is the identifier that flows through the entire chain:

**`tenant` variable → `groups` claim in the JWT → tenant in the RI**

It's the same value all the way through. When an integrator decodes their token and sees `groups: ["org-acme"]`, that `org-acme` is this tenant value.

## Before you run this

Set these two variables:
- `tenant` — the tenant identifier, e.g., `org-acme-corp` (this is exactly what appears in the JWT `groups` claim)
- `tenant_name` — a human-friendly name, e.g., `ACME Corporation`

## What happens

A project role is created in Zitadel with your tenant value. On its own, this does nothing — you still need to create a service account and assign this tenant to it (steps 2-4).

## Under the hood

Zitadel calls this a "project role", and the `flatRoles` action transforms it into the `groups` JWT claim. You don't need to worry about that plumbing — just know that the `tenant` variable you set here is the same value the integrator will see in their token's `groups` array.

# Create a Service Account

This creates a "machine user" in Zitadel — basically a robot account that can authenticate via API (no browser login needed).

## Before you run this

Set these variables:
- `sa_username` — a unique name for the account, e.g., `acme-service-account`
- `tenant_name` — the organisation name (used in the description)

## What happens

- A new machine user is created in Zitadel
- The `sa_user_id` variable is **automatically saved** from the response — you'll need it for steps 3 and 4
- The account can't do anything yet — it still needs credentials (step 3) and a tenant assignment (step 4)

exec: console.log('Service account created — user ID saved: ' + jsonData.userId);

request.description:
# Generate Client Credentials

This creates the username and password (client_id + client_secret) for the service account you just created.

## IMPORTANT — Read this!

The `client_secret` is shown **only once**. If you lose it, you have to run this request again, which **revokes the old secret** (breaking any integrations using it).

## What happens

- `client_id` and `client_secret` are **automatically saved** to your collection variables
- These are the credentials you hand to the integrator
- The integrator uses these to get access tokens from Zitadel

## After running

Copy the `client_id` and `client_secret` from the response and save them somewhere safe. Then share them securely with the integrator.

exec: console.log('Client secret saved to variables (copy it now — shown only once)');

request.description:
# Assign Tenant to Service Account

This is the step that connects the dots. You're telling Zitadel: "This service account belongs to this tenant."

When the service account gets a token, the `tenant` value (e.g., `org-acme`) will appear in the `groups` claim of the JWT. The RI reads `groups[0]` to determine the tenant.

So the chain is: **`tenant` variable → `groups` JWT claim → RI tenant**. Same value, end to end.

## The golden rule

**One service account = one tenant. Always.**

If you assign multiple tenants, the RI just picks the first one, which may not be what you want.

If an integrator needs access to multiple tenants, create a separate service account for each.

## After running

You're done! The integrator now has everything they need:
- `client_id` and `client_secret` (from step 3)
- `project_id` (the Zitadel project ID)
- `zitadel_url` and `ri_url`

Send them these values and point them to the "Integrator" folder.

item.name: Integrator — Authentication & API
item.description:
# Integrator — Authentication & API

This folder is for **integrators** — people who have received service account credentials from an admin and want to call the RI API.

## What you need from your admin

Before you can do anything, you need these four values (set them in the Variables tab):
- `client_id` — your service account username
- `client_secret` — your service account password
- `project_id` — the Zitadel project ID
- `ri_url` — the URL of the Reference Implementation (e.g., `https://ri.labs.pyx.io`)
- `zitadel_url` — the URL of the Zitadel instance (e.g., `https://auth.labs.pyx.io`)

## How to use this folder

1. **Run "Health Check" first** — makes sure the RI is reachable (no auth needed)
2. **Run "Get Access Token"** — swaps your credentials for a temporary token (auto-saved for all other requests)
3. **Run any API request** — List DIDs, List Credentials, etc. They all use the saved token automatically

Tokens last about 12 hours. When yours expires, just run "Get Access Token" again.

## If something goes wrong

- **401 error**: Your token is invalid or expired. Run "Get Access Token" again.
- **403 error**: Your token is valid but has no tenant. Re-run "Get Access Token" and check the Postman Console — if `groups` is null, your admin hasn't assigned a tenant to your service account yet.
- **Can't get a token at all**: Double-check your `client_id`, `client_secret`, and `zitadel_url`.

request.description:
# Get Access Token

**Run this first!** This is your "log in" step. It takes your client_id and client_secret and swaps them for an access token — a temporary pass that lets you call the RI API.

## What happens when you click Send

1. Your credentials are sent to Zitadel
2. Zitadel checks them and returns a JWT (a long encoded string)
3. The token is **automatically saved** to `access_token` — all other requests in this folder use it
4. The console shows you what's inside the token (audience, groups, expiry) so you can verify it looks right

## The three scopes (why they matter)

The request includes three scopes. All three are required — missing any one will break things:

- `openid` — standard login scope, required for all OIDC flows
- `urn:zitadel:iam:org:project:id:{project_id}:aud` — tells Zitadel to put the project ID in the token's `aud` (audience) field. Without this, the RI rejects the token with 401.
- `urn:zitadel:iam:org:projects:roles` — tells Zitadel to include your role grants in the token. Without this, the `groups` claim is missing and the RI can't figure out your tenant (403 error).

## Token lifetime

Tokens last about 12 hours. When yours expires, just run this request again. There's no refresh token for service accounts — you just get a new one.

exec: // Decode and display claims for verification
console.warn('WARNING: Token has no groups claim — API calls will fail with 403.');
console.warn('Check: role grant, scopes, and flatRoles action.');

request.description:
# List DIDs

Fetches all DIDs (Decentralised Identifiers) that belong to your tenant.

This is a good "smoke test" to confirm the whole authentication chain is working. If you get a 200 response (even with an empty list), everything is set up correctly.

## Expected responses

- **200** — success! Returns `{ data: [...], pagination: {...} }`. An empty `data` array is normal for a new tenant.
- **401** — token is invalid or expired. Run "Get Access Token" again.
- **403** — token is valid but your tenant can't be resolved. Re-run "Get Access Token" and check the `groups` claim in the Postman Console output.

exec: console.warn('401 — Token invalid or expired. Run "Get Access Token" again.');
console.warn('403 — Token missing groups claim. Check the Postman Console output from "Get Access Token" to diagnose.');

request.description:
# List Credentials

Fetches all verifiable credentials that belong to your tenant. These are the UNTP credentials (DPP, DIA, DFR, DCC, etc.) that have been issued.

An empty list is normal for a new tenant — credentials appear after you start issuing them through the RI.

exec: console.warn('401 — Token invalid or expired. Run "Get Access Token" again.');
console.warn('403 — Token missing groups claim. Check the Postman Console output from "Get Access Token" to diagnose.');

request.description:
# List Services

Fetches all configured services for your tenant — things like VCKit (credential issuing), storage backends, and identity resolvers.

These are the external services that the RI connects to on behalf of your tenant.

request.description:
# Health Check

A simple "is it alive?" check. No authentication needed.

**Run this first** before trying anything else. If this fails, the RI isn't reachable — check the `ri_url` variable and make sure the service is running.

If this succeeds but other requests fail, the problem is with authentication, not connectivity.
